label: Kingston A. George
narrative: Kingston George is the reason the Big Sur case is worth carrying at all. He identifies himself in the opening paragraph of his 1993 article as the project engineer for the experiments, and everything that makes the case checkable comes from him: the deployment's dates and location, the borrowed Boston University 24-inch telescope on a modified five-inch gun mount owned by the Range Measurements Laboratory of the Air Force Eastern Test Range, the photographs of the team, the name and date of the launch, the sequence of the security reaction, the disposal of the film, and a contemporaneous internal document cited by title and date. He is an interested party against the UFO reading, and he is also the only person in this cluster who both held the access at issue and published about it under his own name. He is careful where a polemicist would not be: he concedes the point about lasers to Jacobs, he describes the classified matter as a weapons-system vulnerability rather than anything exotic, and he records that he himself was questioned along with everyone else. That combination, documented access plus a published concession, is why he is a node and not a footnote.
